summary: A guide from Bob Braden to using IBM's Time Sharing Option (TSO) at UCLA CCN over the network with Telnet. TSO was stable and regularly scheduled but not yet considered production. A user needs a valid charge number and a user ID, and the note says whom to contact.

plainLanguage.summary: This guide explains how network users can log in to UCLA CCN's TSO service. It describes submitting batch jobs, running some programs interactively, and the service's limitations.

subtitle: Instructions for accessing UCLA CCN's IBM Time Sharing Option over the network.

tldr.problem: Users needed instructions for using UCLA CCN's TSO service through the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes two modes: conversational remote job entry and foreground execution, along with login, file and support procedures.
tldr.outcome: TSO was described as stable and regularly scheduled but not yet production; users needed a valid charge number and user ID.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 379 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The guide describes TSO access at CCN in August 1972.

sections.title: TSO Access at CCN
sections.content:
UCLA's IBM Time Sharing Option (TSO) is available at CCN over the network using TELNET. The RFC says it is stable and regularly scheduled, but not yet considered production because restrictions and problems remain.

Users need a valid CCN charge number and a TSO user ID. At the time of the notice, TSO use itself was not charged, though batch jobs submitted from TSO were charged to the user's account.
sections.plainLanguage: Users can reach TSO at UCLA through TELNET. The system was usable but still had restrictions and glitches to resolve.

sections.title: Two Ways to Use TSO
sections.content:
Conversational Remote Job Entry lets a user prepare an OS job stream with EDIT, submit it to batch, check its status and examine output in EDIT. The RFC says TIP users can submit batch jobs this way without using NETRJS through a TENEX machine.

Foreground execution runs some OS/360 programs from the terminal. Its foreground region is limited to 128K, referenced data sets must be on resident disk packs, and execution may be slow because the system time-slices and swaps. The TEST command provides DDT-like debugging, and a user's own program can interact with the terminal.
sections.plainLanguage: Users can submit a batch job and return for its output, or run some programs from the terminal. Foreground programs have memory, storage and speed limits.

sections.title: Files, Login and TELNET Limits
sections.content:
TSO places foreground-created data sets on resident disk packs and catalogs them so users can refer to them by name. At CCN, names use the charge number and user ID as their highest levels. Users can read, write or execute data sets under their charge number, and can rename or remove them.

The RFC says programs could not yet open direct network connections. It refers users to RFC 377 for TELNET access and lists features not then available, including full duplex, lowercase input, special-character translation and optional line-ending choices.
sections.plainLanguage: TSO organizes files by charge number and user ID. The TELNET connection still lacked several features described as planned for a later version.

references.text: RFC 377, Using TSO via ARPA Network Virtual Terminal.
